questions.q: What is the primary lever for buffer pool sizing?
options: The max server memory instance-level setting
The recovery model
The compatibility level
The collation
questions.explain: max server memory caps how much memory SQL Server, including the buffer pool, can use — set too low and the working set won't fit; too high and it starves the OS.

questions.q: Why can instance-wide PLE look healthy while a real problem hides underneath it?
options: On multi-NUMA-node servers, PLE is also tracked per node — one node can be under pressure while the instance-wide aggregate still looks fine
PLE is never tracked per node
Instance-wide PLE is always more accurate than any other measurement
PLE has nothing to do with NUMA nodes
questions.explain: Per-NUMA-node PLE counters can reveal a local imbalance that the instance-wide aggregate masks.

questions.q: After raising max server memory by 8 GB, PLE doesn't improve and PAGEIOLATCH_SH wait time stays the same. What does this tell you, per this lesson?
options: Memory wasn't actually the bottleneck — the investigation should move elsewhere, like I/O or query design
The memory increase definitely helped, just not visibly yet
This result is meaningless and should be ignored
You should immediately add even more memory
questions.explain: A flat PLE and unchanged waits after adding memory is itself useful information: it rules memory out as the constraint.

questions.q: Why shouldn't you compare raw PLE numbers across two servers with very different memory configurations?
options: PLE thresholds genuinely vary by buffer pool size, so the same PLE number doesn't mean the same thing on both
PLE is measured in different units on different servers
PLE can only be measured on one server at a time
There is no relationship between PLE and buffer pool size
questions.explain: A given PLE value represents a different level of health depending on how much memory the buffer pool actually has.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend tracking PLE continuously as part of a monitoring baseline, rather than only checking it when something already feels slow?
options: A single point-in-time PLE reading tells you almost nothing on its own — the trend over time is what reveals whether the buffer pool is actually undersized
PLE can only be queried once per day
Continuous tracking is required by SQL Server licensing
A single reading is always sufficient for diagnosis
questions.explain: Without a baseline trend, you have no way to judge whether a given PLE reading represents a real change or normal variation.
